A new paleomagnetic study in the South Sichuan basin (South China Block) has been carried out on sediments of Early Triassic to Middle Jurassic age. Detailed stepwise thermal and alternating field demagnetizations allowed us to isolate two to three components. A low- temperature component (component A) falls close to the local present Earth field direction. A middle-temperature component (component B) is found both in limestone and red beds of Early Triassic age, in limestones of Middle Triassic age, and finally in red beds of Jurassic age. The component B directions failed the fold test but show a significant increase of the ks/kg ratio at 60% when a progressive stepwise unfolding is applied. The directions obtained at 60% unfolding are grouped best and yield a pole position at 76.5øN, 174.1øE, A95=3.7 ø that is close to the Late Cretaceous pole of the South China Block (SCB) or the Early Tertiary pole of the Eurasian plate. Characteristic directions are finally obtained (component C) for Early Triassic and Early to Middle Jurassic sediments only, both with reversal and fold tests. Characteristic directions are finally obtained (component C) for Early Triassic and Early to Middle Jurassic sediments only, both with reversal and fold tests. They yield pole positions at 44.1øN and 217.2øE (A95=4.9 ø) and 79øN and 227øE (A95-4.5ø), respectively. The Early Triassic result well fits other data of the same age from the SCB. The revised Late Permian to Cretaceous paleopole data provide a new Mesozoic apparent polar wander path for south China. The successive pole positions from Late Permian to Early Triassic indicate motion of the South China Block as a whole rather than local rotations linked to important strain within the block. A new paleomagnetic study in the South Sichuan basin (South China Block) has been carried out on sediments of Early Triassic to Middle Jurassic age. Detailed stepwise thermal and alternating field demagnetizations allowed us to isolate two to three components. A low- temperature component (component A) falls close to the local present Earth field direction. A middle-temperature component (component B) is found both in limestone and red beds of Early Triassic age, in limestones of Middle Triassic age, and finally in red beds of Jurassic age. The strike- continuation can be traced on published maps (Siedlecka et al. 1987; Lutro & Tveten 1996) both westwards towards Fillefjell (Fig. 2) and eastwards to Rondane, a distance of some 120 km. The Olestøl Fault juxtaposes higher tectonostratigraphic units, mostly of the Jotun nappe with lower units in its footwall. Ophiolitic rocks of the Upper Allochthon are preserved in the hanging wall of the Olest øl Fault in the Otta area (Sturt et al. 1991). The ﬁeld relationships and petrography of the fault rocks at both sites on the Olest øl Fault give clear evidence of multiple events on the fault. A single discrete main fault plane cannot be easily identi ﬁed, and fault plane striations are not commonly observed. Systematic kinematic data are not pre- sented here and detailed work is presently underway as a continuation of this study (K. Eig, work in progress). Sampling site 1 (Fig. 2) is located in the fault zone, below the dam at the eastern end of Olefjorden (UTM-832 967). carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: a). All samples (J-39 to 51) where collected along a 26 m section at essentially the same level of the fault zone. Protoliths of the fault rocks are syenitic to monzonitic gneisses very similar to those described above at Olestøl (site 1 & 2). Intrusive relationships between felsic dykes and the gneisses are spectacularly exposed in the cli ﬀs above the fault (Fig. 3a). The network of intrusive veins and dykes makes a good marker for identi ﬁcation of a number of minor faults in a zone 10–50 m above the main fault. Based on comparison with the APWP, and the palaeomagnetic and radiometric data from the fault rocks in western Norway, we assign ages of mid- to late Permian for the HB temperature component and late Jurassic to early Creta- ceous for the LB component respectively. We suggest that the two stages of remanence acquisition were related to important phases of faulting and breccia formation in the Lærdal–Gjende Fault System. The Permian HB magnetizations are most likely related to brecciation and metasomatism as the breccias are character- ized by common epidote veins. The Mesozoic LB components were probably the result of lower temperature thermochemical magnetization (TCRM) of the fault zone. The mode of rema- nence acquisition and some aspects of demagnetization in fault rocks are discussed in Torsvik et al . (1992) and Eide et al . (1997). Summary and conclusions Recent work in western Norway documents a complex tectonic history following the Caledonian orogeny. Based on a number of integrated studies and using a variety of techniques, the post-Caledonian tectonic phases are well de ﬁned and can, in many cases, be directly correlated to o ﬀshore structural fea- tures and tectonics. This previously unnamed fault was, however, identiﬁed as a zone of intense cataclasis and shown in a cross-section by Ridley & Hossack (1986). The strike- continuation can be traced on published maps (Siedlecka et al. 1987; Lutro & Tveten 1996) both westwards towards Fillefjell (Fig. 2) and eastwards to Rondane, a distance of some 120 km. The Olestøl Fault juxtaposes higher tectonostratigraphic units, mostly of the Jotun nappe with lower units in its footwall. Ophiolitic rocks of the Upper Allochthon are preserved in the hanging wall of the Olest øl Fault in the Otta area (Sturt et al. 1991). The ﬁeld relationships and petrography of the fault rocks at both sites on the Olest øl Fault give clear evidence of multiple events on the fault. A single discrete main fault plane cannot be easily identi ﬁed, and fault plane striations are not commonly observed. Systematic kinematic data are not pre- sented here and detailed work is presently underway as a continuation of this study (K. Eig, work in progress). Based on comparison with the APWP, and the palaeomagnetic and radiometric data from the fault rocks in western Norway, we assign ages of mid- to late Permian for the HB temperature component and late Jurassic to early Creta- ceous for the LB component respectively. We suggest that the two stages of remanence acquisition were related to important phases of faulting and breccia formation in the Lærdal–Gjende Fault System. The Permian HB magnetizations are most likely related to brecciation and metasomatism as the breccias are character- ized by common epidote veins. The Mesozoic LB components were probably the result of lower temperature thermochemical magnetization (TCRM) of the fault zone. The mode of rema- nence acquisition and some aspects of demagnetization in fault rocks are discussed in Torsvik et al . (1992) and Eide et al . (1997). Based on a number of integrated studies and using a variety of techniques, the post-Caledonian tectonic phases are well de ﬁned and can, in many cases, be directly correlated to o ﬀshore structural fea- tures and tectonics. Laboratory experiments The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) was measured with a 2 G DC Squid. REHNSTRO } M2 1NGU, Leiv Eiriksonsvei 39, N-7491 Trondheim, Norway (e-mail: trond.torsvik@ngu.no) 2Department of Mineralogy and Petrology, Lund University, So ¨lvegt. 13, S-223 62, Sweden Abstract: A reliable Early Cambrian ( c. 535 Ma) and a preliminary Late Cambrian ( c. 500 Ma) palaeo- magnetic pole from Baltica (Sweden) overlap within uncertainty, and they are also broadly compatible with Vendian ( c. 583 Ma) palaeomagnetic data. Apparent polar wander for Baltica amounts to less than 25/p8between 583 and 500 Ma and, therefore, negates recent speculations that the Earth tipped 90 /p8during the Early Cambrian (true polar wander). Throughout Vendian and Cambrian times, Baltica lay at southerly latitudes ( c. 30–60/p8S). Baltica was geographically inverted, and present-day northern Baltica faced the NW margin of Gondwana which covered the south pole. Laurentia-Eastern Baltica and Laurentia–West Gondwana were separated by the Iapetus Ocean, while the Ægir Sea separated Western Baltica from the Taimyr region of Siberia. During the Cambrian Baltica probably moved eastward along the Gondwana marg

Baltica was geographically inverted, and present-day northern Baltica faced the NW margin of Gondwana which covered the south pole. Laurentia-Eastern Baltica and Laurentia–West Gondwana were separated by the Iapetus Ocean, while the Ægir Sea separated Western Baltica from the Taimyr region of Siberia. Cambrian data from Baltica are pivotal in producing realis- tic palaeogeographic models and to test the IITPW hypothesis, largely because Baltica otherwise o ﬀers some of the best- constrained Late Precambrian and Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic datasets. However, use of Baltican data from the Cambrian has been hampered by unsuitable lithologies with unstable magnetizations and remagnetization problems. These prob- lems are manifested by the large gap in the palaeomagnetic record for 583–480 Ma (Torsvik et al. 1996), hence excluding Baltica from any discussion of the IITPW theory for the Cambrian Period. In this account, we report new palaeomag- netic data from Early and Late Cambrian deposits in northern and southern Sweden (Fig. 1). These data do not support the theory of Cambrian IITPW. We instead utilize the new results to focus on the palaeogeographic implications within a plate-tectonic framework for the Early Palaeozoic. n Received: 28 February 1995 / Accepted: 22 November 1995 Abstract New pole positions for Triassic and Creta- ceous times have been obtained from volcanic and sedi- mentary sequences in Central Iran. These new results confirm the general trend of the Apparent Polar Wan- der Path (APWP) of the Central-East-Iran microplate (CEIM) from the Triassic through the Tertiary as pub- lished by Soffel and Förster (1983, 1984). Two new pal- aeopoles for the Triassic of the CEIM have been ob- tained; limestones and tuffs from the Nakhlak region yield a mean direction of 094.0 7/25.07, N p12, k p4.1, a95p24.77, after bedding correction, corresponding to a palaeopole position of 310.8 7E; 3.9 7S, and volcanic rocks from the Sirjan regions yield a mean direction of 114.57/35.17, N p44, k p45.9, a95p3.27 after bedding correction and a palaeopole position of 295.87E; 10.37N. Combining these with the two previously published re- sults yields a new palaeopole position of 317.5 7E; 12.77N, for the Triassic of the CEIM, thus confirming that large counterclockwise rotations of the CEIM have occurred since the Triassic time. Combining these with the two previously published re- sults yields a new palaeopole position of 317.5 7E; 12.77N, for the Triassic of the CEIM, thus confirming that large counterclockwise rotations of the CEIM have occurred since the Triassic time. New results have also been obtained from Cretaceous limestones from the Saghand region of the CEIM. The mean direction of 340.77/26.37, N p33, k p44.3, a95p3.87, and the corre- sponding palaeopole position of 283.1 7E; 64.4 7N, is in agreement with previously determined Cretaceous pal- aeopole positions of the CEIM. After systematic demag­ netization of representative samples, all other samples would be demagnetized at what was judged to be the 'optimum' field (or fields), averages calculated, and reported with the usual Fisher statistics (Fisher, 1953). These cores were cut into the usual 2.5 cm cylindrical specimens. Palaeomag­ netic measurements were made in two laboratories: at Prince­ ton University, and at the Geological Survey of South Africa in Pretoria. Alternating field demagnetization was the method of choice for all samples. Stepwise demagnetization in 2.5 to 5.0 mT increments was continued up to 30 mT, and in 10 mT steps thereafter, or up to the point where serious Rotational Remanent Magnetism (RRM) problems negated further treat­ ment. Thermal demagnetization was performed on individual specimens from most sites to confirm the carrier of the NRM, and on duplicate specimens from some sites where consistent vectorial results were not obtained. Data were analysed by linear regression (Kirschvink, 1980; see representative Zijder­ veld diagrams in Appendix) and averages calculated by Fisher and Bingham statistics (Onstott, 1980). Previous palaeomagnetic work The wide distribution of the Karoo basaltic rocks made them the subject of some of the earliest palaeomagnetic studies undertaken in Africa (e.g. Graham & Hales, 1957; Graham et al., 1962; Van Zijl et al., 1962; see also Nairn, 1960). In the early work, alternating field (A.F.) demagnetization - if attempted at all - was rarely carried to very high fields and usually was applied in batch fashion. After systematic demag­ netization of representative samples, all other samples would be demagnetized at what was judged to be the 'optimum' field (or fields), averages calculated, and reported with the usual Fisher statistics (Fisher, 1953). The early studies reported were mostly local and geographically scattered. Despite this, remarkably similar pole positions were usually obtained (see Table 1). More recent (and experimentally robust) palaeomagnetic studies of Karoo igneous rocks were those of Gidskehaug et al. (1975) and Henthorn (1981) (Table 1). Gidskehaug et al.'

These cores were cut into the usual 2.5 cm cylindrical specimens. Palaeomag­ netic measurements were made in two laboratories: at Prince­ ton University, and at the Geological Survey of South Africa in Pretoria. Alternating field demagnetization was the method of choice for all samples. Stepwise demagnetization in 2.5 to 5.0 mT increments was continued up to 30 mT, and in 10 mT steps thereafter, or up to the point where serious Rotational Remanent Magnetism (RRM) problems negated further treat­ ment. Thermal demagnetization was performed on individual specimens from most sites to confirm the carrier of the NRM, and on duplicate specimens from some sites where consistent vectorial results were not obtained. Data were analysed by linear regression (Kirschvink, 1980; see representative Zijder­ veld diagrams in Appendix) and averages calculated by Fisher and Bingham statistics (Onstott, 1980). Conclusions This study supports the contention that the bulk of the Karoo Igneous Province was emplaced very rapidly, largely during one single polarity epoch, about 183 Ma ago. The volcanism was virtually contemporaneous over most of southern Africa and can be correlated with similar volcanic activity in Antarc­ tica. Two palaeomagnetic poles were determined for the Karoo volcanic rocks from the extensive database now available. A particularly robust palaeopole position at latitude = -69.2, longitude= 98.3, k = 416, a = 3.3 for Karoo Volcanic Prov­ ince at 183 ± 5 Ma has been calculated. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: J 99R Integrated U-Pb geochronology and palaeomagnetic study of mafic to felsic volcanic rocks of the Derdepoort Belt of South Africa are employed to test the hypothesis that the Pilbara and Kaapvaal Cratons were joined as part of a Late Archaean 'Vaalbara' supercontinent. An age of 2782 ± 5 Ma is deduced for eruption of the Derdepoort basalts, bracketed by a con­ cordant SHRIMP zircon age of 2781 ± 5 Ma for overlying felsic volcanics and a concordant isotope dilution zircon age of 2783 ± 2 Ma for underlying granite of the Gabarone Complex. Based on the low (subgreenschist) metamorphic grade of the basalts, the presence of highly stable single domain magnetite, and a positive conglomerate test, the magnetization of the Derdepoort basalts is inferred to date from the time of their emplacement and cooling at 2782 Ma. Results yield a primary palaeopole at 005 ° E, 40° S (A95 = 18° ), and indicate a palaeolatitude of 64.5 ± 17.5 ° for the Kaapvaal Craton at 2782 Ma. Published palaeomagnetic data for the Mount Roe Basalts of the Pilbara Craton indicate a palaeolatitude of 34.3 ± 6.4° at 2772 ± 2 Ma. Box 147, Liverpool, L69 3BX Synopsis The Tertiary igneous succession of Arran is poorly known, partly because of a paucity of informative field relationships, so palaeomagnetic polarities and Ar-Ar dates have been measured to provide additional constraints. New palaeomagnetic results for over 200 sites have been combined with published data. The Northern Granite has normal polarity (N), while the later Central Ring Complex has reversed polarity (R). All sampled quartz-porphyries are N and all felsites (apart from some intermediate direction (I) sites) are R, the only known correlations between polarity and petrography in the British Tertiary Igneous Province. The remaining petrographic types may be found with either polarity. All dykes sampled on the NW coast are N, as are 70% of those on the NE coast, but elsewhere R polarity predominates. Radiometric dates show that the activity occurred approximately 61 to 58 Ma ago. It spanned at least the magnetic polarity sequence R-N—R, and although additional polarity intervals cannot be ruled out, a tentative succession consistent with R-N-R and with as few as possible recurrences of petrographic types has been constructed. Introduction and synopsis of geology The object of this paper is to use palaeomagnetism and, to a lesser extent, radiometric dating to improve the knowledge of the stratigraphy of the Tertiary igneous rocks of Arran and thence to deduce how long the activity continued. Originally, it was hoped that small differences in palaeomagnetic directions could be used to correlate different igneous bodies, as has some­ times been achieved elsewhere

fers from other complexes of the BTIP in having the widespread occurrence of intermediate members of the calc-alkaline series. Unlike most of the other Scottish centres, where basic lavas are abundant, the only basic lavas now found in Arran are remanie masses in a subsided caldera within the Central Ring Complex where, presumably, they escaped erosion. Minor intrusions are very common in Arran. Over a thousand dykes have been recorded, chiefly around the coasts. They mostly trend NW-SE to N-S (Knaap 1973). The other common minor intrusions are sills, which are found in Permo-Triassic sediments in the southern half of the island. Petrographic types found in these minor intrusions are analcime-olivine-dolerites (crinanites), olivine-dolerites, tholeiitic-dolerites, quartz-dolerites, quartz-porphyries, felsites and pitch- stones (Tyrrell 1928), plus augite-diorite microgranite and microgranophyre in the Tighvein 'complex' (Herriot 1975). The oldest track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. This mode of movement was terminated at the onset of the Isan Orogeny. The oldest track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent with the interpretation that this trail was caused by the movement of the plate over a thermal anomaly in the upper mantle. section_candidates.excerpt: ndaries in the northern Australian superbasins and to the initiation of sub- basins that host the base-metal deposits. Most bends are also associated with magnetic overprints related to episodes of fluid circulation, and three appear to be associated with the expulsion of metal- rich brines that formed the world-class Broken Hill, Mt Isa and HYC Pb–Zn deposits. According to the pole path, the movement of the region in the period 1730–1590Ma can be described as series of clockwise-counterclockwise rotations about mostly similar Euler poles located southwest of Australia, suggesting that the lithosphere may have been coupled alternately to oppositely convecting cells in the mantle. This mode of movement was terminated at the onset of the Isan Orogeny. The oldest track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent with the interpretation that this trail was caused by the movement of the plate over a thermal anomaly in the upper mantle. Most bends are also associated with magnetic overprints related to episodes of fluid circulation, and three appear to be associated with the expulsion of metal- rich brines that formed the world-class Broken Hill, Mt Isa and HYC Pb–Zn deposits. According to the pole path, the movement of the region in the period 1730–1590Ma can be described as series of clockwise-counterclockwise rotations about mostly similar Euler poles located southwest of Australia, suggesting that the lithosphere may have been coupled alternately to oppositely convecting cells in the mantle. This mode of movement was terminated at the onset of the Isan Orogeny. The oldest track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent with the interpretation that this trail was caused by the movement of the plate over a thermal anomaly in the upper mantle. ndaries in the northern Australian superbasins and to the initiation of sub- basins that host the base-metal deposits. Most bends are also associated with magnetic overprints related to episodes of fluid circulation, and three appear to be associated with the expulsion of metal- rich brines that formed the world-class Broken Hill, Mt Isa and HYC Pb–Zn deposits. According to the pole path, the movement of the region in the period 1730–1590Ma can be described as series of clockwise-counterclockwise rotations about mostly similar Euler poles located southwest of Australia, suggesting that the lithosphere may have been coupled alternately to oppositely convecting cells in the mantle. This mode of movement was terminated at the onset of the Isan Orogeny. The oldest track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent with the interpretation that this trail was caused by the movement of the plate over a thermal anomaly in the upper mantle. Most bends are also associated with magnetic overprints related to episodes of fluid circulation, and three appear to be associated with the expulsion of metal- rich brines that formed the world-class Broken Hill, Mt Isa and HYC Pb–Zn deposits. According to the pole path, the movement of the region in the period 1730–1590Ma can be described as series of clockwise-counterclockwise rotations about mostly similar Euler poles located southwest of Australia, suggesting that the lithosphere may have been coupled alternately to oppositely convecting cells in the mantle. This mode of movement was terminated at the onset of the Isan Orogeny. The oldest track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent with the interpretation that this trail was caused by the movement of the plate over a thermal anomaly in the upper mantle. Most bends are also associated with magnetic overprints related to episodes of fluid circulation, and three appear to be associated with the expulsion of metal- rich brines that formed the world-class Broken Hill, Mt Isa and HYC Pb–Zn deposits. According to the pole path, the movement of the region in the period 1730–1590Ma can be described as series of clockwise-counterclockwise rotations about mostly similar Euler poles located southwest of Australia, suggesting that the lithosphere may have been coupled alternately to oppositely convecting cells in the mantle. This mode of movement was terminated at the onset of the Isan Orogeny. The oldest track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent with the interpretation that this trail was caused by the movement of the plate over a thermal anomaly in the upper mantle. According to the pole path, the movement of the region in the period 1730–1590Ma can be described as series of clockwise-counterclockwise rotations about mostly similar Euler poles located southwest of Australia, suggesting that the lithosphere may have been coupled alternately to oppositely convecting cells in the mantle. This mode of movement was terminated at the onset of the Isan Orogeny. The oldest track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent with the interpretation that this trail was caused by the movement of the plate over a thermal anomaly in the upper mantle. KEY WORDS: apparent polar wander path,McArthur Basin,Mt Isa Inlier,palaeomagnetism,Palaeo- proterozoic. section_candidates.excerpt: ndaries in the northern Australian superbasins and to the initiation of sub- basins that host the base-metal deposits. Most bends are also associated with magnetic overprints related to episodes of fluid circulation, and three appear to be associated with the expulsion of metal- rich brines that formed the world-class Broken Hill, Mt Isa and HYC Pb–Zn deposits. According to the pole path, the movement of the region in the period 1730–1590Ma can be described as series of clockwise-counterclockwise rotations about mostly similar Euler poles located southwest of Australia, suggesting that the lithosphere may have been coupled alternately to oppositely convecting cells in the mantle. This mode of movement was terminated at the onset of the Isan Orogeny. The oldest track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent with the interpretation that this trail was caused by the movement of the plate over a thermal anomaly in the upper mantle. This mode of movement was terminated at the onset of the Isan Orogeny. The oldest track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent with the interpretation that this trail was caused by the movement of the plate over a thermal anomaly in the upper mantle. section_candidates.excerpt: ndaries in the northern Australian superbasins and to the initiation of sub- basins that host the base-metal deposits. Most bends are also associated with magnetic overprints related to episodes of fluid circulation, and three appear to be associated with the expulsion of metal- rich brines that formed the world-class Broken Hill, Mt Isa and HYC Pb–Zn deposits. According to the pole path, the movement of the region in the period 1730–1590Ma can be described as series of clockwise-counterclockwise rotations about mostly similar Euler poles located southwest of Australia, suggesting that the lithosphere may have been coupled alternately to oppositely convecting cells in the mantle. This mode of movement was terminated at the onset of the Isan Orogeny. The oldest track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent with the interpretation that this trail was caused by the movement of the plate over a thermal anomaly in the upper mantle. LABORATORY METHODS AND MAGNETIC PROPERTIES Thirty-three block-orientated samples were collected from mafic and tonalitic granulite, metadolerite and granitic dykes, using a sun compass for sample orientation. Eighty- eight cylindrical specimens (25 mm diameter) were drilled from the sampled blocks. The palaeomagnetic and magnetic anisotropy study has been carried out in the palaeo- magnetic laboratory of the Tectonics Special Research Centre at the University of Western Australia. Magnetic remanence was measured using a 2G755R cryogenic mag- netometer . At least one specimen from each block was sub- jected to stepwise thermal demagnetisation using MMTD2 furnaces manufactured by Magnetic Measurements (~10 nT residual field). Also at least one specimen from each block was subjected to stepwise alternating field (AF) demag- netisation using a 2G600 automated degaussing system. The results obtained from the pilot collection were used for determining the demagnetisation intervals and for the number of steps to be used for the remaining specimens. Magnetic susceptibility was measured after each heating step with a MS2 susceptibility meter . Isothermal remanent magnetisation (IRM) experiments were carried out using a MMPM9 pulse magnetiser . A complex deformation history during high-grade meta- morphism is recorded in the Bremer Bay area. Northwest- verging folds and thrusts, along with southeast-verging ‘back-thrusts’, indicate northwest–southeast contraction during convergence between East Antarctica and the Yilgarn Craton. Northeast-striking normal shear zones and widespread boudinage (especially of mafic layers) indicate subsequent subhorizontal northwest–southeast extension. The Bremer Bay region of the Albany Mobile Belt was chosen as its deformation history is well constrained by U/Pb SHRIMP and Rb/Sr geochronology (Black et al. 1992). The consistency of palaeomagnetic results of Early Cambrian dolerite dykes throughout the Albany Mobile Belt (Harris & Li 1995) has shown that there has been negligible tilting during breakup between Western Australia and Antarctica. This study sought to determine a palaeomagnetic pole for these high-grade rocks and late dykes for com- parison to the Australian apparent polar wander path. The Australian apparent polar wander path for the Mesopro- terozoic (Idnurm & Giddings 1988) is presently constrained by a small number of studies, the majority of which have concerned northern and central Australia. Magnetic anisotropy was also measured in order to determine how magnetic fabric relates to regional strain and thus to indirectly establish the timing for acquisition of the magnetic fabrics. Yilgarn Craton from the East Determination of magnetic anisotropy and a ca 1.2 Ga palaeomagnetic pole from the Bremer Bay area, Albany Mobile Belt, Western Australia S. A. PISAREVSKY AND L. B. HARRIS* Tectonics Special Research Centre, Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Western Australia, Crawley, WA 6009, Australia. Granulite facies tonalitic gneiss, mafic granulite and late metadolerite dykes from Bremer Bay in the Mesoproterozoic Albany Mobile Belt yield palaeomagnetic remanence that were acquired between ca 1.2 Ga and 1.1 Ga. A well-constrained pole (66.6°N, 303.7°E) fits the ca 1.2 Ga part of the Precambrian Australian apparent polar wander path. This pole is in agreement with the high- latitude position of Australia at ca 1.2–1.1 Ga shown on some Rodinia reconstructions. More data are required before any significance can be attributed to a second, poorly defined pole (41.8°S, 243.7°E) that falls at some distance from the ca 0.8 Ga part of the Australian apparent polar wander path. Magnetic anisotropy measurements from all samples except late granite dykes indicate northeast– southwest elongation (i.e. parallel to the local trend of the orogenic belt) and northwest–southeast contraction. This is in agreement with the orientation of principal strain axes deduced from structures

on and the dominant shallowly northwest-plunging minimum fabric axes (orientation of maximum shortening) determined from AMS measure- ments (Figure 12d). The northwest strike of the younger normal shear zones is again in agreement with a shallow , northeast–southwest maximum extension direction. Normal shearing is consistent with AMS measurements that show a steeper orientation of minimum fabric axes (Figure 12a). 110 S. A. Pisarevsky and L. B. C, Carboniferous; P , Permian; Tr , Triassic; K, Cretaceous; J, Jurassic. Three specimens from granite dykes (as shown in Figure 3b) show quite different directions of AMS axes (Figure 12b). This may be due to the younger age of these dykes, which post-date penetrative deformation. However , more samples must be studied to confirm this suggestion and to determine the regional structural significance of the magnetic fabric. ion of C. A BB2 single-polarity component has been isolated in seven samples of mafic granulites (Figure 14). No system- atic differences in magnetic characteristics [NRM, mag- netic susceptibility , Q ratio, SIRM and (BO) CR] of these samples and mafic granulites with BB1 direction have been found. BB2 component is rather scattered (Figure 6b) and absent in tonalitic gneiss, dolerite and granite. Mean directions, statistics and pole positions for BB1 and BB2 components are given in Table 1. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS Figure 15 shows the palaeomagnetic poles for BB1 and BB2 components together with the 1200–600 Ma fragment of the Australian apparent polar wander path (Idnurm & Giddings 1988; Idnurm et al. 1995) and fragments of the Phanerozoic Australian apparent polar wander path (Harris & Li 1995). The BB1 pole (66.6°N, 303.7°E) fits the ca 1.2 Ga part of Precambrian Australian apparent polar wander path. However , this particular part is poorly deter- mined as some of the earlier poles it is based on have been revised (Tanakah & Idnurm 1994) and other poles have poor age constraints. The closeness of this part of the Australian apparent polar wander path to the Late Palaeo- zoic Australian apparent polar wander path must also be considered. LABORATORY METHODS AND MAGNETIC PROPERTIES Thirty-three block-orientated samples were collected from mafic and tonalitic granulite, metadolerite and granitic dykes, using a sun compass for sample orientation. Eighty- eight cylindrical specimens (25 mm diameter) were drilled from the sampled blocks. The palaeomagnetic and magnetic anisotropy study has been carried out in the palaeo- magnetic laboratory of the Tectonics Special Research Centre at the University of Western Australia. Magnetic remanence was measured using a 2G755R cryogenic mag- netometer . At least one specimen from each block was sub- jected to stepwise thermal demagnetisation using MMTD2 furnaces manufactured by Magnetic Measurements (~10 nT residual field). Also at least one specimen from each block was subjected to stepwise alternating field (AF) demag- netisation using a 2G600 automated degaussing system. The results obtained from the pilot collection were used for determining the demagnetisation intervals and for the number of steps to be used for the remaining specimens. Magnetic susceptibility was measured after each heating step with a MS2 susceptibility meter . Isothermal remanent magnetisation (IRM) experiments were carried out using a MMPM9 pulse magnetiser . A complex deformation history during high-grade meta- morphism is recorded in the Bremer Bay area. Northwest- verging folds and thrusts, along with southeast-verging ‘back-thrusts’, indicate northwest–southeast contraction during convergence between East Antarctica and the Yilgarn Craton. Northeast-striking normal shear zones and widespread boudinage (especially of mafic layers) indicate subsequent subhorizontal northwest–southeast extension. HARRIS* Tectonics Special Research Centre, Department of Geology and Geophysics, University of Western Australia, Crawley, WA 6009, Australia. Granulite facies tonalitic gneiss, mafic granulite and late metadolerite dykes from Bremer Bay in the Mesoproterozoic Albany Mobile Belt yield palaeomagnetic remanence that were acquired between ca 1.2 Ga and 1.1 Ga. A well-constrained pole (66.6°N, 303.7°E) fits the ca 1.2 Ga part of the Precambrian Australian apparent polar wander path. This pole is in agreement with the high- latitude position of Australia at ca 1.2–1.1 Ga shown on some Rodinia reconstructions. More data are required before any significance can be attributed to a second, poorly defined pole (41.8°S, 243.7°E) that falls at some distance from the ca 0.8 Ga part of the Australian apparent polar wander path. Magnetic anisotropy measurements from all samples except late granite dykes indicate northeast– southwest elongation (i.e. parallel to the local trend of the orogenic belt) and northwest–southeast contraction. The volcanic–siliceous complex is composed of tectonic blocks closely associated with the ophiolites. This complex consists of lava ﬂows, lava breccias, tuffs, and cherts. The volcanics are calc-alkaline basalts to basaltic andesites, that formed in an ensimatic island arc (Kravchenko- Berezhnoy 1989; Chekhovich et al . 1990; Kravchenko-Berezhnoy & Nazimova 1991). We have studied paleomagnetically lithotectonic units of different ages forming the Karaginsky accretionary prism in order to assess the rotation of the geological blocks forming the island struc- ture, in the horizontal plane, to estimate whether these blocks were involved in the strike-slip move- ments during the different periods of the island structure formation. Results from the Cretaceous Espina Basalts of the Calatuigas Ophiolite in the South Palawan Block (SPB) pass a fold test, yield normal and reversed directions with a magnetic intensity and AF demagnetization characteristics consistent with a primary TRM. The mean direction is 293.9 8 and an inclination of 5.8 8, with a k of 37.7 and an a95 of 12.6 8. This suggests that these ophiolites have moved northward and rotated counterclockwise by 66 82 +138 with respect to the geocentric axial dipole (GAD) ﬁeld. It also suggests that they were obducted from the south. Paleomagnetic directions from the Jurassic Busuanga Cherts and the Cretaceous Guinlo Formation from the island of Busuanga in the North Palawan Block (NPB) and from the Guinlo on the main island of Palawan are similar, fail regional fold tests, and have AF demagnetization characteristics consistent with secondary magnetization. Their inclinations are statistically indistinguishable at a 95% signiﬁcance level, but variation in declination suggests di erential local rotation about a vertical axis. The paleolatitude is comparable to that of regions of pervasive Cretaceous remagnetization in the South China borderland and may reﬂect similar remagnetization, consistent with the NPB’s proposed South China origin. # 2000 Elsevier Science Ltd. Paleomagnetic methods Standard collection and analysis methods were used throughout the study. About eight samples were col- lected per site with a gasoline powered drill. In some cases, when the rock was too friable, too fractured, or too hard to drill satisfactorily in the ﬁeld, hand samples were collected and cores drilled from them in the laboratory. The measurements of magnetization were made on a 2G TM RF SQUID superconducting magnetometer and with a Molspin TM spinner magnet- ometer. Fisher (1953) statistics and Kirschvink (1980) principal component analysis were utilized. AF demagnetization was carried out with a 2G TM demagnetizer. Stepwise and continuous systems devel- oped at University of California at Santa Barbara (e.g. Dunn and Fuller, 1984 and Fuller, 1987) were used for thermal demagnetization. In presenting the Zijderveld data (Zijderveld 1967), we have adopted the procedure of classifying the results into subsets and giving their representation at the various sites. The paleomagnetic results also permit a paleolatitude of 2.5 8 S and a lar- ger CW rotation because of the equatorial indetermi- nacy of polarity by declination alone. However, we prefer the interpretation of the smaller rotation which is comparable with that observed by Shibuya et al. (1991) in the Celebes Sea. 1983), deposited shortly after a Paleoproterozoic glaciation of perhaps global extent (Evans et al., 1997; Tsikos and Moore, 1998; Kirschvink et al., 2000). Together the iron - and manganese -rich cycles constitute the Early Paleoproterozoic Hotazel Formation, with an age of ca. 2200 Ma (Cornell et al., 1996) or 2400 .Ma (Bau et al., 1999). The Hotazel Formation lies conformably between the underlying Ongeluk lavas and the overlying dolomitic Mooidr aai Formation. The strata are very gently folded, dipping westward 5° to 15° throughout the Kalahari manganese field. Two main ore types are present in the Kalahari manganese deposit (Cairncross et al., 1997): low -grade carbonate-rich Mamatwan-type ore (30 and 39 wt % Mn) and high -grade oxide-rich Wessels-type ore (>42 wt % Mn). Low-grade Mamatwan -type ore (Kleyenstüber, 1984; Nel et al., 1986) constitutes 97 percent of the total ore reserves and may be described as a microcrystalline (grain sizes below 10 um), finely laminated mudstone composed of kutnahorite (CaMn(C0 3)2), first-generation braunite (Mn 7Si012), and hematite (I; roman numerals in parentheses denote order of generation). Low-grade Mamatwan -type ore (Kleyenstüber, 1984; Nel et al., 1986) constitutes 97 percent of the total ore reserves and may be described as a microcrystalline (grain sizes below 10 um), finely laminated mudstone composed of kutnahorite (CaMn(C0 3)2), first-generation braunite (Mn 7Si012), and hematite (I; roman numerals in parentheses denote order of generation). Abundant millimeter -sized ovoids of kutnahorite, recrystallized hematite (Ib), and braunite occur in this microcystalline matrix, which is thought to be of sedimentary or early diagenetic origin (Kleyenstüber, 1984). Together the iron - and manganese -rich cycles constitute the Early Paleoproterozoic Hotazel Formation, with an age of ca. 2200 Ma (Cornell et al., 1996) or 2400 .Ma (Bau et al., 1999). The Hotazel Formation lies conformably between the underlying Ongeluk lavas and the overlying dolomitic Mooidr aai Formation. The strata are very gently folded, dipping westward 5° to 15° throughout the Kalahari manganese field. Two main ore types are present in the Kalahari manganese deposit (Cairncross et al., 1997): low -grade carbonate-rich Mamatwan-type ore (30 and 39 wt % Mn) and high -grade oxide-rich Wessels-type ore (>42 wt % Mn). (Lüders et al., 1999) and mass -balance calculations (Gutzmer and Beukes, 1997) have illustrated that upgrading of manganese ore from Mamatwan to Wessels type occurred within a l ow-temperature (<250°C) hydrothermal metasomatic system by residual enrichment of Mn at the expense of Mg, Ca, C0 2, and Si0 2. It has previously been uncertain if hematite (I) and late diagenetic and/or metamorphic hausmannite (I) were consumed during this alteration, because both minerals occur widely in both altered and unaltered ores. The Mashonaland and Hartley igneous units are broadly coeval-possibly consanguineous with the poorly dated Sibasa basalt (Soutpansberg Group) and Sand River dikes (Barton and Pretorius, 1997)and related to the ca. 19 00 Ma rift stage of a Wilson cycle (Cornell et al., 1998). Our MAM -2 pole lies just beyond the Mashonaland and Hartley results along the apparent polar wander path (Fig. 6A; Evans et al., in press) and so may result from extension-related magmatism that ex pelled stratabound fluids into the Kalahari manganese field. Alternatively, MAM -2 could be due to foreland-driven orogenic fluids from the Kheis fold thrust episode (Gutzmer and Beukes, 1996), loosely dated at 1700 to 1800 Ma (Stowe, 1983; Cornell et al., 1998). Both the rift - and Kheis -related tectonic models for MAM -2 would be consistent with the various crosscutting relationships observed in the Kalahari manganese field (Gutzmer and Beukes, 1996). GFF , Vol. 123 (Pt. 4, December), pp. 205–215. Stockholm. ISSN 1103-5897. Abstract: The 1.85–1.67 Ga Transscandinavian Igneous Belt (TIB) forms a major Paleoproterozoic igneous complex in the western part of the Fennoscandian Shield. Different tectonic models propose that the TIB was formed in a tectonic regime governed either by compression or by extension. This paper presents an analysis of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) and paleomagnetic data from the Rätan granite (1.70 Ga), which forms a large pluton in the central part of the TIB. The major aim of the study is to test the existing tectonic models and to de- fine a paleomagnetic pole position for the Rätan granite. Three contrast- ing magnetic fabric domains are identified. In the eastern and western domains the AMS fabric is characterized by NW–SE to N–S trending subvertical foliation planes and a girdle distribution of the maximum and intermediate anisotropy axes. The central domain is characterized by subhorizontal magnetic foliation planes and lineations that cluster in a NW–SE trending direction. We

he central domain is characterized by subhorizontal magnetic foliation planes and lineations that cluster in a NW–SE trending direction. We suggest that the Rätan granite was emplaced in a tectonic regime governed by NW–SE directed extension and that the pluton was fed obliquely with a magma source situated to the present northwest. A positive baked contact test is demonstrated for a basic dyke suggesting that the Rätan granite has not been re-magnet- ized since c. 1.6 Ga. A paleomagnetic formation mean direction is de- fined for the granite (decl. = 2°, incl. = 59°) that yields a paleopole posi- tion of Plat = 67° and Plon = 190°. Elming, Division of Applied Geophysics, Luleå University of Technology, SE-971 87 Luleå, Sweden, hakan.mattsson@ sb.luth.se. Manuscript received 5 February 2001. Revised manuscript accepted 23 August 2001. The Transscandinavian Igneous Belt (TIB) forms a major Late Paleoproterozoic igneous complex in the Fennoscandian Shield. The TIB was formed at c. 1.85–1.67 Ga (Ahl et al. 1999) along the southwestern boundary of the Svecofennian Domain (Gaál & Gorbatschev 1987). It defines a belt of igneous rocks that ex- tends

e-mar- gin process (e.g. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova 1993), and plate tectonic models proposed that the TIB was formed in a tectonic regime governed by compression (Windley 1993). However, Ahl et al. (1999) present a model suggesting that the Dala granit- oids in the central part of the TIB were formed in a period of tran- sition between subduction-related compression (1.81–1.77 Ga) and an extensive environment (1.70–1.68 Ga). The Rätan granite (e.g. Lundegårdh 1967; Lundqvist 1968), which forms a large intrusion north and east of the Dala granitoids, was emplaced at c. 1.70 Ga (U–Pb, Wilson et al. 1985; Patchett et al. 1987; Delin 1996). GFF , Vol. 123 (Pt. 4, December), pp. 205–215. Stockholm. ISSN 1103-5897. Abstract: The 1.85–1.67 Ga Transscandinavian Igneous Belt (TIB) forms a major Paleoproterozoic igneous complex in the western part of the Fennoscandian Shield. Different tectonic models propose that the TIB was formed in a tectonic regime governed either by compression or by extension. This paper presents an analysis of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) and paleomagnetic data from the Rätan granite (1.70 Ga), which forms a large pluton in the central part of the TIB. The major aim of the study is to test the existing tectonic models and to de- fine a paleomagnetic pole position for the Rätan granite. Three contrast- ing magnetic fabric domains are identified. In the eastern and western domains the AMS fabric is characterized by NW–SE to N–S trending subvertical foliation planes and a girdle distribution of the maximum and intermediate anisotropy axes. The Tecomazuchil Formation was sampled in stratigraphic order over a total height of 13 m in 11 beds, and magnetostratigraphic results have already been published (Urrutia-Fucugauchi et al., 1990). The Morelos Formation was sampled in 8 beds covering a total thickness of 18 m. Roughly 50 km further to the south, the Rosario Formation was sampled in 12 beds with a total thickness of 7 m. Sampling was done in stratigraphic order, taking 3–4 cores per horizon to check for the internal consistency of the magnetic record. In this manner 31 cores from the Morelos lime- stone were obtained, 38 cores from the Tecomazuchil sandstone, and 35 cores from the Rosario Formation. The Tecomazuchil Formation was sampled in stratigraphic order over a total height of 13 m in 11 beds, and magnetostratigraphic results have already been published (Urrutia-Fucugauchi et al., 1990). The Morelos Formation was sampled in 8 beds covering a total thickness of 18 m. Roughly 50 km further to the south, the Rosario Formation was sampled in 12 beds with a total thickness of 7 m. Here the overlaying Tecocoyunca Group has been studied as well, but the paleomagnetic results showed strong, unremovable secondary overprints and were therefore of no tectonic relevance (Bo ¨hnel, 1985). Sampling was done in stratigraphic order, taking 3–4 cores per horizon to check for the internal consistency of the magnetic record. In this manner 31 cores from the Morelos lime- stone were obtained, 38 cores from the Tecomazuchil sandstone, and 35 cores from the Rosario Formation. Since there is no younger early Paleozoic paleomagnetic pole yet available for the Argentine Precordillera, its kinematic history between the Early Cambrian and the Late Ordovician remains unconstrained by paleo- magnetic data. The recent acquisition of paleomagnetic data from Paleozoic rocks of this region, albeit still scarce, permit establishment of some constrains on the tectonic and paleogeographic evolution of some of these terranes. A reliable paleomagnetic pole from the Early Cambrian Cerro Totora Formation in northern Precordillera confirms that the Argentine Precordillera is an exotic terrane that was part of or adjacent to Laurentia, very likely at the Ouachita Embayment, in the Early Cambrian. Paleomag- netic poles from an Early Ordovician magmatic belt in northwest Argentina permit the identification of a peri-Gondwanic–rotated terrane, called the Eastern Puna–Famatina terrane, with volcanic arc affinities. The polarity option for the Fen pole remains an important and open question due to recent suggestions of a true polar wander event in the mid- Cambrian; however, we consider that the south polarity option offers the simplest tectonic model for the rifting of Rodinia and opening of the Iapetus Ocean between Baltica and Laurentia. Finally, we note the similarity of the Fen paleomagnetic pole to paleomagnetic poles of Permo-Triassic age in Baltica and urge caution in the unequivocal use of the Fen pole as primary until further substantiated by coeval poles from Baltica. This section outcrops along the Kulumbe river, where sediments with an age ranging .from the Vendian Uppermost Precambrian to the Ordovician are exposed over a distance of about 10 km. These deposits are tilted 15 8 to 208 towards the .east. Mikutskiy and Petrakov 1961 and Kravtsov .1967 believe that folding of the beds occurred in .the Carboniferous, while Groisman 1970 and .Malich 1975 consider that the folding may have continued until the Triassic. Rock magnetic studies identify annealed metamorphic magnetite grains with multidomain properties as the remanence carriers; a widely recorded stable remanence was probably ﬁxed by grain shape e ects. Granulite facies terranes are typically between one and two orders more strongly magnetised than amphibolite terranes and AMS fabrics correlate mostly with metamorphic mineral fabrics observed in the country rocks. Progressive thermal demagnetisation identiﬁes a range of two and three component structures resident in magnetite. An important component recognised as a partial or complete remagnetisation by Late Mesozoic–Tertiary tectonic/magmatic activity is present in basement at the southern margin of the outcrop (Miyun terrane) and where extensive granite plutonism has occurred (Zhunhua terrane). These components have directions corresponding to remanence in the Yunmeng Shan Granite (119–114 Ma, D/I = 33/58 8, 39 samples, a 95 = 3.58, palaeopole at 2018E, 64 8N).

Granites generated during late stages of suturing into the eastern Asian continental collage were emplaced as plutons into the metamorphic basement during Cretaceous times; they constitute the last major thermal event to inﬂuence this region. The present paper is con- cerned mainly with the latter three inliers. Within a ca. 1000200 km area extending from southern Inner Mongolia in the west to Hebei Province in the east (Fig. 1) basement outcrop averages some 75–85% gneisses and 15–25% supracrustal sediments (Qian et al., 1985). Medium to high grade polymetamorphic terranes occur along the northern margin of the Huabei (North China) Shield as inliers exposed beneath supracrustal successions comprising the Meso-Neoproterozoic Jixian Supergroup. Cooling of these terranes and their elevation to present surface levels occurred prior to de- position of the oldest part of the Jixian succession at 01850 Ma. Introduction Although the kinematics of the major Shields during Precambrian times is quantiﬁed by palaeomagnetic study, the recoverable record is always incomplete, both because the rock record is itself only sporadically preserved, and because later overprinting can obscure an ancient remanence record. The present Precambrian palaeomagnetic database is mostly derived from study of intense, but generally brief, igneous episodes and platformal successions of Meso- and Neoproterozoic age. The oldest palaeomagnetic record in each shield is preserved in the underlying basement rocks. This base- ment typically comprises a polymetamorphic gneiss complex produced by crustal accretion and repeated reworking during Archaean and Early Proterozoic times. Introduction Although the kinematics of the major Shields during Precambrian times is quantiﬁed by palaeomagnetic study, the recoverable record is always incomplete, both because the rock record is itself only sporadically preserved, and because later overprinting can obscure an ancient remanence record. The present Precambrian palaeomagnetic database is mostly derived from study of intense, but generally brief, igneous episodes and platformal successions of Meso- and Neoproterozoic age. The grains contributing to this e ect have para- magnetic and ferromagnetic properties; the paramagnetic minerals are mostly the iron-bearing sili- cates whilst the ferromagnetic contribution is from magnetite, and sometimes pyrrhotite or hematite. The strong ferromagnetic e ect of the small volume of these latter grains is often much larger than the para- magnetic and (weak negative) diamagnetic e ects of the bulk silicate matrix. Whilst the inﬂuence of fabric on the dilute amounts of ferromagnetic grains in which the stable remanence resides cannot be isolated by study of AMS, it is a useful qualitative indicator of bias of magnetic remanence by fabric; a comparison between results from samples of strong and weak fab- rics at the same site is often able to recognise the likely importance of any such bias. They have not been considered as priorities for palaeomagnetic study owing to age and orientation uncertainties. These latter are, however, mostly small and the intrusions are therefore targets for investigation because suitable stratigraphic units are so few (and essentially limited to the EVG and BVG). The intrusions tend to be magnetically less stable than equivalent volcanics (Morris, 1973; Piper et al., 1978, the Carrock Fell Layered Gabbros are a notable exception) probably because they are more commonly dominated by larger magnetite grain sizes and multi domains. Higher failure rates therefore accompany these studies and some samples have a remanence dominated by Recent ﬁeld components. Nevertheless, numerous intrusive igneous samples show a coherent remanence structure unobscured by Variscan or later overprinting and it is with these components that the present study is primarily concerned. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Palaeomagnetic study of intrusive igneous rocks, including application of thermal demagnet- ization, ﬁeld tests and principal component analysis, identiﬁes a history of Ordovician to Devonian magnetization. Late plutons (Shap and Skiddaw granites and/or aureoles) record a shallow dipolar (A3) axis (mean declination/inclination (D=I 278= 178) dating from emplacement in late Early Devonian times ( c. 395 Ma). Although this axis is recorded as a sporadic overprint in older rocks, no pervasive remagnetization is attributable to batholith emplacement. Instead, the Carrock Fell Complex Layered Gabbros have a mid- to late Ordovician (A1) remanence ( D=I 174=ÿ 5818, 36 samples, a95  488) predating regional F2 folding. Later events in this igneous complex comprise the Carrock Fell Granophyre with a post-folding Ordovician remanence, and Round Knott Dolerite with a remanence linked to hydrothermal alteration late in the Ordovician magmatic episode. A Late Ordovician (Ashgill) palaeoﬁeld is also deﬁned by remanence (A2) in the Threlkeld–St John’s Microgranite and aureole (438 Ma, D=I 2365=6338, 41 samples, a95  478). he ﬁnal phase of subduction-related magmatism at this margin of Avalonia. Following cessation of volcanism, a transgressing sea deposited limestones, shales, mudstones and greywackes between Late Caradoc and Ludlow times. This succession forms the Winderemere Supergroup and makes up the Silurian outcrop in Figure 1. During burial and subsequent Acadian deformation the Lower Palaeozoic rocks of the Lake District were metamorphosed to no higher than lower greenschist grade, in common with the paratectonic Caledonides of Wales; this was insucient to comprehensively remagnetize pre-Acadian rocks which are reported widely to retain an Ordovician remanence record (Briden and Morris, 1973; Piper et al., 1978; Piper, 1979; Channell and McCabe, 1992). In addition to the basic plutonism noted above, acidic magmatism occurred at various stages between the intense mid-Ordovician volcanic events and the culmination of tectonic activity in the Acadian episode. A general distinction is recognized between earlier Na-rich activity and later more K-rich activity (Piper et al., 1978). The Carrock Fell and Ennerdale Granophyres are typical sub-volcanic plutons, whilst the Threlkeld– St John’sbody is a microgranite with small phenocrysts of plagioclase and pyroxene suggesting near-liquidus compositions (O’Br

ents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. The Carrock Fell Complex was the subject of earlier study employing a.f. demagnetization and endpoint analysis (Briden and Morris, 1973; Morris, 1973). Since the complex was then considered to be a post-tectonic event, the data were evaluated in situ; more recent evidence shows that the layered gabbros predate F2 folding (Roberts, 1971; Harris and Dagger, 1987). Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. he ﬁnal phase of subduction-related magmatism at this margin of Avalonia. Following cessation of volcanism, a transgressing sea deposited limestones, shales, mudstones and greywackes between Late Caradoc and Ludlow times. This succession forms the Winderemere Supergroup and makes up the Silurian outcrop in Figure 1. During burial and subsequent Acadian deformation the Lower Palaeozoic rocks of the Lake District were metamorphosed to no higher than lower greenschist grade, in common with the paratectonic Caledonides of Wales; this was insucient to comprehensively remagnetize pre-Acadian rocks which are reported widely to retain an Ordovician remanence record (Briden and Morris, 1973; Piper et al., 1978; Piper, 1979; Channell and McCabe, 1992). A general distinction is recognized between earlier Na-rich activity and later more K-rich activity (Piper et al., 1978). Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. PIPER Geomagnetism Laboratory, Department of Earth Sciences, University of Liverpool, Liverpool L69 7ZE, UK The Lake District terrane of northern England comprises Upper Cambrian–Silurian sediments and volcanics accumulated at the northern margin of the Avalonian Plate during growth and demise of the Iapetus Ocean. Ocean closure and suturing resulted in Late Ordovician and Acadian tectonism and were accompanied by emplacement of a large regional batholith. tholith. Palaeomagnetic study of intrusive igneous rocks, including application of thermal demagnet- ization, ﬁeld tests and principal component analysis, identiﬁes a history of Ordovician to Devonian magnetization. Late plutons (Shap and Skiddaw granites and/or aureoles) record a shallow dipolar (A3) axis (mean declination/inclination (D=I 278= 178) dating from emplacement in late Early Devonian times ( c. 395 Ma). Although this axis is recorded as a sporadic overprint in older rocks, no pervasive remagnetization is attributable to batholith emplacement. Instead, the Carrock Fell Complex Layered Gabbros have a mid- to late Ordovician (A1) remanence ( D=I 174=ÿ 5818, 36 samples, a95  488) predating regional F2 folding. Later events in this igneous complex comprise the Carrock Fell Granophyre with a post-folding Ordovician remanence, and Round Knott Dolerite with a remanence linked to hydrothermal alteration late in the Ordovician magmatic episode. A Late Ordovician (Ashgill) palaeoﬁeld is also deﬁned by remanence (A2) in the Threlkeld–St John’s Microgranite and aureole (438 Ma, D=I 2365=6338, 41 samples, a95  478). Other intrusions carrying a remanence predating the Acadian deformation include the Great Cockup Picrite (458 Ma, D=I 432=ÿ 3188, 31 samples, a95  778) and ba

he ﬁnal phase of subduction-related magmatism at this margin of Avalonia. Following cessation of volcanism, a transgressing sea deposited limestones, shales, mudstones and greywackes between Late Caradoc and Ludlow times. This succession forms the Winderemere Supergroup and makes up the Silurian outcrop in Figure 1. During burial and subsequent Acadian deformation the Lower Palaeozoic rocks of the Lake District were metamorphosed to no higher than lower greenschist grade, in common with the paratectonic Caledonides of Wales; this was insucient to comprehensively remagnetize pre-Acadian rocks which are reported widely to retain an Ordovician remanence record (Briden and Morris, 1973; Piper et al., 1978; Piper, 1979; Channell and McCabe, 1992). In addition to the basic plutonism noted above, acidic magmatism occurred at various stages between the intense mid-Ordovician volcanic events and the culmination of tectonic activity in the Acadian episode. A general distinction is recognized between earlier Na-rich activity and later more K-rich activity (Piper et al., 1978). The Carrock Fell and Ennerdale Granophyres are typical sub-volcanic plutons, whilst the Threlkeld– St John’sbody is a microgranite with small phenocrysts of plagioclase and pyroxene suggesting near-liquidus compositions (O’Br

ents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. We report U–Pb ages and palaeomagnetic results for two suites of maﬁc sills within the intracratonic Bangemall Basin of Western Australia, one of which is dated at 1070 ± 6 Ma and carries a high-stability palaeomagnetic remanence. Comparison of the Bangemall palaeopole with Laurentian data suggests that previous reconstructions of eastern Australia against either western Canada (SWEAT) or the western United States (AUSWUS) are not viable at 1070 Ma. This implies that the Paciﬁc Ocean did not form by separation of Australia–Antarc- tica from Laurentia, and that up to 10 000 km of late Neoproterozoic passive margins need to be matched with other continental blocks within any proposed Rodinia supercontinent. The characteristic high-temperature remanence component (B-component) exhibits predominantly reverse polarity, and is generally separable by thermal demagnetization temperature steps between 350 and 580‡C. This B-component can also be isolated by alternating fields (AFs) cleaning at a peak value of 20^30 mT using a hybrid thermal^AF demagnetization method. Two major folding events occurred, presumably during the Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous and during the Early Ju- rassic to Middle Jurassic, corresponding to the Variscan and Indosinian orogenies, respectively. Indeed, two unconformities can be distinguished in the Alashan/Hexi Corridor terrane, the earlier one between Late Devonian and Early Carbon- iferous sediments, and the later one between Early Jurassic and Middle Jurassic sediments [17]. The Carboniferous system is made up in as- cending order of the Lower Carboniferous Chou- niugou Formation, Middle Carboniferous Jin- gyuan and Yanghugou Formations, and the Upper Carboniferous Taiyuan Formation (Fig. 2). The Lower Carboniferous series unconform- ably overlies the Upper Devonian Zhongning Formation. It is mainly composed of sandy sand- stone and mudstone interbedded with limestone or light-gray and gray limestone. Two major folding events occurred, presumably during the Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous and during the Early Ju- rassic to Middle Jurassic, corresponding to the Variscan and Indosinian orogenies, respectively. Indeed, two unconformities can be distinguished in the Alashan/Hexi Corridor terrane, the earlier one between Late Devonian and Early Carbon- iferous sediments, and the later one between Early Jurassic and Middle Jurassic sediments [17]. The Carboniferous system is made up in as- cending order of the Lower Carboniferous Chou- niugou Formation, Middle Carboniferous Jin- gyuan and Yanghugou Formations, and the Upper Carboniferous Taiyuan Formation (Fig. 2). The Lower Carboniferous series unconform- ably overlies the Upper Devonian Zhongning Formation. It is mainly composed of sandy sand- stone and mudstone interbedded with limestone or light-gray and gray limestone. The upper part of this series yields corals (e.g. Yuanophyllum kan- suense, Dibunophyllum bristolens ), brachiopods (Gigantoproductus maxima , Kansuella kansuensis ) and £ora (e.g. Sublepidodendron mirabile , Rhodea hsianghsiangensis), indicating a late Datang age (i.e. late Visean stage, [17]). Two major folding events occurred, presumably during the Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous and during the Early Ju- rassic to Middle Jurassic, corresponding to the Variscan and Indosinian orogenies, respectively. Indeed, two unconformities can be distinguished in the Alashan/Hexi Corridor terrane, the earlier one between Late Devonian and Early Carbon- iferous sediments, and the later one between Early Jurassic and Middle Jurassic sediments [17]. The Carboniferous system is made up in as- cending order of the Lower Carboniferous Chou- niugou Formation, Middle Carboniferous Jin- gyuan and Yanghugou Formations, and the Upper Carboniferous Taiyuan Formation (Fig. 2). The Lower Carboniferous series unconform- ably overlies the Upper Devonian Zhongning Formation. It is mainly composed of sandy sand- stone and mudstone interbedded with limestone or light-gray and gray limestone. The upper part of this series yields corals (e.g. Yuanophyllum kan- suense, Dibunophyllum bristolens ), brachiopods (Gigantoproductus maxima , Kansuella kansuensis ) and £ora (e.g. Sublepidodendron mirabile , Rhodea hsianghsiangensis), indicating a late Datang age (i.e. late Visean stage, [17]). The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. Paleomagnetic data show that the TRM was separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician, and then drifted northward. The TRM was sutured to Siberia and Kazakstan blocks during the Permian, however, the composite Mongolia-NCB block did not collide with Siberia till Late Jurassic. The suturing zone was located at northern latitude of 25" where the two blocks collided at the western part in the Late Triassic. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. The TRM was sutured to Siberia and Kazakstan blocks during the Permian, however, the composite Mongolia-NCB block did not collide with Siberia till Late Jurassic. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. The TRM was part of Gondwanaland, and might be close to the YZB and Australia in the Early Paleozoic. Paleomagnetic data show that the TRM was separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician, and then drifted northward. The TRM was sutured to Siberia and Kazakstan blocks during the Permian, however, the composite Mongolia-NCB block did not collide with Siberia till Late Jurassic. The NCB and YZB collided first in the eastern part where they were located at northern latitude of about 6"-8', and a triangular oceanic basin remained in the Late Permian. The suturing zone was located at northern latitude of 25" where the two blocks collided at the western part in the Late Triassic. The NCB was probably independent in terms of dynamics. its drift history was dominant by latitudinal placement ac- companying rotation in the Early Paleozoic. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. The TRM was part of Gondwanaland, and might be close to the YZB and Australia in the Early Paleozoic. Paleomagnetic data show that the TRM was separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician, and then drifted northward. The TRM was sutured to Siberia and Kazakstan blocks during the Permian, however, the composite Mongolia-NCB block did not collide with Siberia till Late Jurassic. During Late Permian to Late Triassic, the NCB and YZB were characterized by northern latitudinal placement and ro- tation on the pivot in the Dabie area. The NCB and YZB collided first in the eastern part where they were located at northern latitude of about 6"-8', and a triangular oceanic basin remained in the Late Permian. The suturing zone was located at northern latitude of 25" where the two blocks collided at the western part in the Late Triassic. The NCB was probably independent in terms of dynamics. its drift history was dominant by latitudinal placement ac- companying rotation in the Early Paleozoic. The YZB was close to Gondwanaland in Cambrian, and separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician. The TRM was part of Gondwanaland, and might be close to the YZB and Australia in the Early Paleozoic. Paleomagnetic data show that the TRM was separated from Gondwanaland during the Late-Middle Ordovician, and then drifted northward. The TRM was sutured to Siberia and Kazakstan blocks during the Permian, however, the composite Mongolia-NCB block did not collide with Siberia till Late Jurassic. During Late Permian to Late Triassic, the NCB and YZB were characterized by northern latitudinal placement and ro- tation on the pivot in the Dabie area. The NCB and YZB collided first in the eastern part where they were located at northern latitude of about 6"-8', and a triangular oceanic basin remained in the Late Permian. The suturing zone was located at northern latitude of 25" where the two blocks collided at the western part in the Late Triassic.
